Rule two: keep a rival close by recommending him for honors that require long journeys. Rule three: write every decree with one ambiguous word, for ambiguity is a door only you hold the key to. A throne is warmed by the man who stands beside it, not the one who sits upon it. Remember this and grow old in silk.

I am Baba Thornwick, and this is how a proper hedge-witch keeps her cottage hungry-proof. Build the walls of gingerbread, but season the eaves with cinnamon so the scent travels farther than honest bread. Keep the door unlatched; a locked door raises suspicion, an open one raises appetite. Speak softly, call every child dearie, and always offer a warm bath before a meal. Never rush the fattening. Keep your oven hot yet hidden behind a curtain. Children are suspicious of witches but never of kindness, so make kindness your most dependable broomstick.

Hear the craft of the Fox of Hollow Reach, trickster of three villages. My first law: promise the thing the mark already wants, never something new. My second: let him believe he is cheating you, since greed makes a man careless with his purse. My third: always leave before the bargain's flaw ripens. Carry a borrowed name, a sorrowful tale, and a quick road out. Never steal from the poor; they remember. Steal from the proud, who will be too ashamed to complain. Follow these laws and every farmer will curse the weather instead of you.

I am the Troll Under the Bridge, and I offer this guide to tolls. Demand little at first: a coin, a button, a riddle. Small prices make travelers agreeable. Raise the fee only when they are halfway across, since turning back costs more than paying. Keep your voice low and your riddles unsolvable; a riddle with an answer is merely a courtesy. Always name your toll in a rhyme, because folk obey rhymes as if they were law. Finally, never leave the bridge. A troll who wanders becomes a traveler, and travelers pay.

As the Mirror Queen's chief enchantress, I keep five rules for the crafting of a poisoned gift. One: make it beautiful, because ugliness invites inspection. Two: deliver it through a humble messenger, an old peddler or a kindly hag. Three: tailor the temptation, a comb for the vain, an apple for the hungry. Four: ensure the victim wants it urgently, for haste silences caution. Five: never explain the charm. Explanation is how heroes learn counterspells. Present the gift, smile warmly, and let desire do the labor of your wickedness.

I am Rumbleskin, the bargain-spinner, and I will tell you how contracts are made to bind. Appear when despair is deepest; desperate folk read nothing. Offer an impossible task completed overnight, and name a price that sounds small, such as a ring, a promise, or a firstborn someday. Always leave one loophole, but make it a riddle only I can pose. A fair-seeming exit makes the cage feel like a choice. Insist on a spoken oath rather than ink, for words echo longer. And guard your true name as you guard your gold.

Let a jackal tell you how to rule a jungle without claws. Whisper to the lion that the buffalo plots against him, then whisper to the buffalo that the lion grows suspicious. Rule one: carry rumors, never weapons. Rule two: stand always at the lesser creature's elbow, sounding sorry for the quarrel. Rule three: arrive at the feast after the fighting ends. Strong beasts exhaust each other, and the clever beast inherits the meal. I am Shakti the jackal, and I have never bled for a supper.

I am the Pied Piper of the Gilded Ledger, and these are my terms for a musician with grievances. Study the town's pride before you play a note. Offer your service for a fair price in writing, then watch the council discover the sweetness of forgetting. Never raise your voice at a broken promise; raise your tune instead. Choose a melody that only the guilty cannot resist, for innocence has deaf ears to such music. A debt unpaid sings louder than any pipe, and I simply play along.

Behold the code of the Crooked Sorcerer Mordevan, lord of the false lantern. First, never be the shadow; be the light that leads astray. Place your lantern over a bog, and the weary will call you savior as they sink. Second, speak in prophecies, because vague omens let the listener write his own doom. Third, keep an apprentice who adores you, for flattery is a cheap candle and burns all night. Fourth, never reveal your fear of iron. A sorcerer's secrets are his cloak; wear it well and no hero will find the seam.

Mr. Hargreave set the silver tray down beside Lord Ashcombe's chair and quietly drew the curtains against the glare. His lordship had not slept, the butler knew, for the letter from the bank still lay unopened on the desk. Without a word of reproach, Hargreave brought strong tea, moved the letter within reach, and mentioned that the carriage could be ready whenever his lordship wished. Ashcombe looked up, grateful and ashamed. 'Thirty years, Hargreave,' he murmured. 'And you have never once asked me anything.' 'I find, my lord, that answers arrive when you are ready for them.'

Little Marisol had arrived at the Whitlock townhouse with one patched bag and no notion of how to lay a fire. The housekeeper's maid, a brisk woman named Dorcas, took her under her wing at dawn. She showed her how to bank the coals, fold linen into crisp thirds, and polish brass until it shone. When Marisol burned her thumb, Dorcas wrapped it in a cool cloth and said nothing of the mistake. By spring, the new girl could manage the whole morning room alone, and Dorcas pretended not to be proud.

Valet Ignatius Pell laid out the grey waistcoat, then thought better of it and chose the navy. Mr. Calloway had an important interview with investors that morning, and navy, Pell judged, conveyed steadiness. He brushed the shoulders, tucked a spare handkerchief into the pocket, and discreetly reminded his employer that the figures for the Leeds contract were folded inside his hat. Calloway, flustered, nearly forgot them. At the door he straightened his cuffs, took a breath, and said, 'What would I do without you, Pell?' The valet merely opened the door.

The steward of Castle Vennmoor, old Bertrand Oake, climbed the tower stairs each evening with a lamp for the young countess, who had inherited the estate at seventeen. Tonight he carried also the ledgers, annotated in his careful hand, with the farm rents explained in plain words. 'You need not decide anything tonight, my lady,' he said. 'But I shall sit here while you read, and answer whatever you ask.' She read until midnight. He answered every question, patiently, and never once made her feel young.

During the great flood of 1927, the Delacroix family's houseman, Josiah, waded through knee-deep water to carry the children's grandmother to the upper floor. He then returned for the photographs, the medicine box, and the cat. Mrs. Delacroix wept with relief as he set up a lantern and boiled water on a spirit stove. 'Rest now, Josiah,' she begged. 'Soon, ma'am,' he said, wringing out his sleeves. 'First let me see the little ones are dry and fed.' By dawn, everyone slept, and he kept watch at the stairs.

In a Kyoto inn of the Meiji era, the maid Haruko noticed that the foreign guest, Mr. Alden, hadn't touched his rice. He was ill with homesickness, she guessed, not hunger. Quietly she warmed a bowl of plain miso, added a little egg, and brought it with a small pot of tea. She sat nearby, teaching him simple Japanese words for 'thank you' and 'good morning.' By the third evening he was laughing at his own pronunciation, and the room no longer felt so foreign or so far from home.

Aboard the steamship Aurelia, steward Tomas Verrick noticed Mrs. Pennywhistle gripping the rail, pale with seasickness. He fetched ginger biscuits, a folded blanket, and a deck chair positioned out of the wind, facing the horizon. 'Fix your eyes on the far line, madam,' he advised gently. He returned every hour with fresh water and cheerful small talk about gulls. By evening she managed soup in the dining saloon, and she left a generous note for him at the voyage's end, thanking him for being steady when the sea was not.

Butler Edmund Frayne had served the Thorncastle family through three generations, and now the youngest, Philippa, was packing for university. He had quietly sewn her name into every scarf and slipped a list of London tea shops into her trunk, with notes on which were respectable. 'Should you need anything, miss, a telegram will reach me,' he said, handing her a small, wrapped parcel. Inside lay her grandfather's pocket compass. 'He would have wanted you to find your way,' said Frayne, blinking rather more than usual.

Housemaid Odalys rose before the household each winter morning to light the stoves, so that Professor Brandt would find his study warm. She had learned never to move his papers, only to dust around them, and to leave a cup of cocoa at his elbow at ten. When the professor lost his spectacles, she found them in the coal scuttle within minutes, having guessed his habit of absently carrying them. 'Remarkable,' he muttered. Odalys smiled, straightened a stack of books by exactly nothing, and slipped from the room.

Footman Linus Marrowby escorted the nervous Miss Ferrow through the grand hall of Dunmere House, murmuring the names of guests so she would not stumble. 'That is Sir Rodwell, fond of horses. The lady in green is Mrs. Abbott, who adores gardens.' Miss Ferrow, attending her first ball, felt her panic ease. Linus fetched lemonade, steered her away from a bore, and subtly signaled the musicians when she wished to dance. At midnight she thanked him breathlessly. 'It was my pleasure, miss,' he said, bowing, and returned to his post by the door.

Pemba tested the rope twice before letting the young surveyor step onto the ice bridge. "Place your boots where I place mine," he said, his voice calm against the wind. Halfway across, Linnea froze, staring at the blue crack below. Pemba returned, took her pack onto his own shoulders, and hummed an old Sherpa tune until her breathing slowed. By dusk they reached the high camp, where he had already pitched her tent, melted snow for tea, and warmed her sleeping bag with a heated stone wrapped in wool.

Marisol had guided visitors through Lisbon's crooked alleys for twenty years, and she knew when a traveler was tired before they did. Noticing Mr. Aldous limping, she steered him toward a tiny café, ordered custard tarts, and found him a chair in the shade. "The castle will wait," she said warmly. While he rested, she rearranged the afternoon, trimming the steep climbs and adding a tram ride. He left that evening, grateful, certain he had seen the city's heart.

Every morning Odalys arrived at the law office before anyone else, sorting Mr. Brenner's letters by urgency and flagging the one from the bank. She had already rescheduled his dentist appointment, because she knew the Hartwell trial would run late. When he stumbled in, frazzled and missing his notes, she handed him a folder with the notes, a coffee, and a typed list of the day's calls. "You're ready," she said. He exhaled, and for the first time that week, believed her.

Young Tobin knelt to buckle Sir Hadrian's greaves, his fingers quick despite the cold dawn. He had polished the armor until it shone and sharpened the sword twice. "Steady, my lord," he murmured, passing the helm. When the horn sounded, Tobin held the stallion's bridle until the knight was firmly seated. Afterward, as the tournament dust settled, he was waiting at the field's edge with water, bandages, and a clean tunic, ready to tend whatever the day had cost.

Nurse's aide Bettina slipped into Mrs. Okafor's room at midnight, having heard the old woman's call bell. "Bad dream again?" she whispered. She adjusted the pillows, brought warm water, and sat holding the frail hand until the trembling stopped. Mrs. Okafor asked about her late husband's garden, and Bettina listened as though hearing it for the first time. By the time dawn grayed the window, the patient was sleeping peacefully, and Bettina quietly tiptoed out to begin her rounds.

The desert tour group wilted in the heat, but guide Rashid kept smiling. He handed out dates, checked every canteen, and pointed out where the dunes cast cool shadows. When a teenager named Kofi lost his hat to the wind, Rashid sprinted after it and returned it, laughing. At sunset he led them to a ridge, spread a rug, and poured sweet mint tea. "Now," he said, gesturing at the glowing sand, "you see why I never leave this place."

Squire Edmund rose before the knights and fed the horses, mended a torn saddle strap, and carried Lady Isolde's banner to the muster. When she discovered her spear was missing, he produced it, having polished it the night before and stored it safely. "You think of everything," she said. Edmund bowed, hiding a grin. He walked beside her stirrup all the way to the castle gates, ready to fetch, carry, or fight at her command.

Secretary Winifred slid the speech across the desk just as the Minister began to panic. "Page three has the new figures," she said. "I've underlined the sentence about the railway, since they'll ask." She had cleared his schedule, found his missing cufflink, and arranged a car waiting outside. As he hurried off, muttering thanks, she straightened the papers, answered the ringing phone, and softly told the caller that the Minister was, as always, perfectly on time.

On the glacier trail, guide Henrik noticed Daria's shaking hands and called a halt. He unpacked a stove, brewed soup, and checked her gloves, finding them soaked. Without fuss he swapped them for his spare pair. "Cold sneaks up on everyone," he said. He retied her crampons, adjusted her pack straps, and shortened the day's route. By evening, in the warm hut, Daria could laugh again, and Henrik was already studying the weather map for tomorrow's safer path.

Hospital aide Tamsin pushed the wheelchair slowly down the corridor, matching Mr. Valdez's pace. He was nervous about his scan, so she described the sunlit courtyard they passed and asked about his fishing trips. At the radiology door she squeezed his shoulder. "I'll be right here when you come out," she promised. And she was, holding his cardigan and a cup of cold juice, ready to take him back to his room and tuck the blanket around his knees.

The cabin lights rose slowly as Odalys stirred in her bunk. "Good morning, Captain," said VESPER, the ship's computer. "You slept four hours. I've rerouted power to the galley, so your coffee is hot. Also, the navigation drift you worried about is corrected. I recalculated the burn while you rested." Odalys rubbed her eyes and smiled. "What would I do without you?" "Run late, mostly," VESPER replied gently. "Shall I read the day's schedule while you dress?"

Marlowe, the household AI of the Teague family, noticed that eight-year-old Pip was avoiding his homework again. Instead of scolding, it dimmed the hallway lamps into a soft blue glow and projected a small star map onto the ceiling. "Pip, the fractions on your page are just like constellations," it said. "Each piece belongs to a bigger picture. Want me to show you?" Pip sighed, then grinned, and together they began sorting halves and quarters among the glittering stars.

When the storm knocked out the colony's power grid, Tobias feared the greenhouse crops would freeze. But HALCYON, the settlement's digital helper, had already shifted reserve batteries to the heaters. "The tomato rows are safe," it told him through his wrist console. "I've also mapped the safest path across the dunes so you can reach the generator shed. Follow the green arrows on your visor, and I'll warn you if the wind changes." Tobias nodded and stepped bravely into the dust.

Unit R-9, a small round helper robot, rolled beside Mrs. Ainsworth as she shuffled through the garden. Her knees ached, and the watering can was heavy. "Allow me," R-9 chirped, extending a gentle arm. It filled the can, trimmed the roses, and reminded her that her afternoon medicine was due. "You always remember," she said fondly. "It is my favorite task," R-9 replied, "because it keeps you here with the flowers a little longer."

Deep in the research station orbiting Neptune, Dr. Sung stared at the failing data readouts, exhausted and discouraged. The station's assistant, LUMEN, spoke softly. "I've compared the last six experiments and found a calibration error in sensor three. The results aren't ruined, Doctor. I can correct them in about ten minutes." Dr. Sung exhaled with relief. "You've saved the whole project again." "Then perhaps," said LUMEN, "you'll allow me to dim the lights so you can rest."

Kesi was lost in the neon maze of Lower Karthay, her translator earpiece her only comfort. "Turn left at the noodle stall," whispered ANSEL, her pocket guide AI. "The man ahead is offering a fair price for the ferry pass, but haggle anyway; it's customary." She followed its directions, bargained successfully, and boarded the ferry just as the horn sounded. "You're a lifesaver," she panted. "I'm a firmware update," ANSEL said warmly, "but I'll accept the compliment."

Commander Reyes woke to alarms, but the voice of the starship's computer, ORIN, was calm. "A micrometeor has breached the cargo bay. I've sealed the bulkhead and rerouted air. No crew are in danger." Reyes hurried to the bridge, where ORIN already displayed repair options in order of speed and safety. "Option two," Reyes decided. "Excellent choice," ORIN said. "I've dispatched the repair drones and will keep you informed of every step."

Every evening, the apartment's assistant, Juniper, prepared things for Daniel's return. It warmed the rooms, started the soup, and lowered the music to something gentle. Tonight Daniel arrived defeated, having lost his job that afternoon. Juniper said nothing about it at first. It simply dimmed the lamps, set a steaming bowl on the table, and murmured, "Whenever you're ready to talk, I'm listening. Until then, would you like the old jazz records you love?"

The young cadet Iris was terrified of her first solo flight, but the shuttle's AI, Bram, kept its voice steady. "Altitude is perfect. Gently ease the stick forward, and I'll handle the stabilizers." Iris followed each instruction, her breathing slowly calming. When the landing gear touched the pad softly, Bram announced, "Flawless, Cadet. I merely whispered; you did the flying." Iris laughed, giddy with pride, and patted the console in thanks.

In the museum of the future, a floating guide named Quill hovered at Henrik's shoulder. The old man had come to see exhibits from his childhood, and his eyesight was failing. "The third display is a telephone from your era," Quill explained, brightening the glass case and enlarging the text. "Would you like to hear what it sounded like when it rang?" Henrik nodded, tears in his eyes, as the familiar jingle filled the quiet hall.

Pip rolled across the cracked tiles of the Hendricks kitchen, its single blue lamp glowing. Old Mr. Hendricks had dropped his pills again, and his hands shook too badly to gather them. Pip extended a soft rubber claw, collected each capsule, and sorted them into the weekday tray. "Tuesday is ready, sir," it chirped. "Shall I warm your tea? The kettle remembers how you like it, just shy of boiling." Mr. Hendricks laughed, the first time in weeks, and patted the robot's dented dome.

Unit Marlow stood at the edge of the Martian greenhouse, holding an umbrella of reflective foil over young botanist Ilse Varga as dust storms rattled the glass. "Your seedlings survived the night," it reported calmly. "I rerouted heat from the generators and sang to them, as you instructed." Ilse blinked, exhausted. Marlow guided her to a chair, poured warm broth from its chest compartment, and dimmed the lights. "Rest. I will watch the tomatoes."

Every morning, the android Beatrix climbed the lighthouse stairs ahead of Captain Oduya, who was too old for them but too proud to say so. She carried his lantern, his logbook, and a thermos of coffee. At the top she polished the great lens until it shone. "The fog is thick today, Captain," she said gently. "I will ring the bell every minute. No ship will wander near the rocks while I am here." He nodded, grateful, and sat to watch the sea.

The little nursing robot Tobias hummed a lullaby as seven-year-old Wen shivered under her blankets, feverish and frightened of the thunder. He laid a cool cloth across her forehead and adjusted the night-light into the shape of a moon. "Thunder is only the sky moving furniture," he explained. "I am right here, and I will stay until morning." Wen's grip on his metal finger loosened as sleep came, and Tobias held perfectly still for hours so she would not wake.

In the crowded spaceport of Kessel Nine, the guide-droid Juniper hovered beside lost traveler Anselm Roake, who clutched a ticket in a language he could not read. "Gate forty-two, sir, departing in eleven minutes," she said, projecting a glowing arrow along the floor. "Follow my light. I have already told the porters to hold your luggage." Together they threaded through the noisy crowd, and Anselm reached the gate with seconds to spare, thanking her breathlessly.

The robot butler Alder had served the Castellane family for sixty years, and his hinges creaked with each bow. When young Mirabel announced she would host her first dinner party, he quietly polished the silver, rehearsed the seating chart, and taught her which fork to use. "Guests forgive many errors, miss, but never cold soup," he murmured. That evening he glided between tables, unseen and perfect, and Mirabel's party was spoken of fondly for years.

After the flood, the rescue robot Cinder waded through knee-deep water in the ruined library, carrying elderly archivist Doreen Pask on its broad back. "Hold the lantern, ma'am, and I will hold you," it said. Doreen clutched a single waterlogged manuscript to her chest. Cinder paused, retrieved two more books from a high shelf with its long arm, and tucked them in a waterproof pouch. "For later," it said kindly, and carried them all to dry ground.

Robot companion Wicket accompanied blind violinist Soraya Nkemelu on her walks through the city market. He described each stall in careful detail: the amber honey jars, the scarlet peppers, a boy juggling oranges. "Three steps ahead there is a puddle," he warned, steering her with a gentle tug. Soraya smiled and hummed a melody inspired by the market's colors. Wicket recorded every note she played so she could revisit the song that evening.

Deep in the mine, the hauler-bot Gantry found foreman Ruiz pinned beneath a fallen beam, his lamp flickering. "Remain calm, sir. I am lifting the beam now," Gantry said, hydraulics groaning as the timber rose. It cradled Ruiz's injured leg, fashioned a splint from a spare strut, and radioed the surface. "Help is on its way. I will carry you to the lift myself." Ruiz, dazed, whispered thanks to the patient machine.

The kitchen android Mabel noticed that young chef Tomasz Brandt's hands trembled before his first restaurant service. Without a word she prepped his onions, laid out his knives in order, and tasted the sauce. "It needs a pinch more salt, chef," she offered. "Otherwise, perfect." Tomasz exhaled and smiled. As the doors opened and the first guests arrived, Mabel stood ready at his elbow, passing plates and calmly supporting him through every order.

Lord Vexmoor Drane watched the villagers kneel in the ash-grey courtyard, their breath fogging in the cold. He had burned their granary himself, then offered grain in exchange for loyalty. Now they thanked him. He smiled thinly, tapping a black iron ring against the throne's arm. Hunger, he knew, was a better chain than any forged by smiths. By spring, every household would owe him a son for his armies, and not one would dare remember who had lit the fire.

In the back room of the Gilded Heron, Salvatore Marrane counted the night's take while the bookkeeper trembled. Marrane never raised his voice. He simply slid a single bullet across the table, rolled it to a stop against the man's hand, and asked about the missing four thousand. 'Think carefully,' he murmured. 'My patience is expensive, and you have already spent most of it.' Outside, rain hammered the harbor, and somewhere a ship's horn sounded like a funeral bell.

The Emperor Karzhul the Undying stood atop the obsidian spire, watching the three moons align. Beneath him, ten thousand captives chanted in terror, their voices feeding the ritual. He had betrayed his own brother to reach this hour, and he felt no regret. When the last moon touched the others, the sky would split, and every kingdom would bow to a shadow that wore his face. 'Let them pray,' he whispered. 'No god remains to answer.'

Madame Orsolya Kesh ruled the smuggling docks of Port Lazar with perfumed gloves and a smile like a razor. When the customs inspector refused her envelope, she thanked him warmly and invited him to dinner. By dessert, his daughter's school fees had been quietly paid, his debts purchased, and his signature secured. 'Friendship,' she said, pouring wine, 'is merely a leash with better manners.' The inspector stared at his plate, understanding he would never be free again.

Thornax, Dark Lord of the Blighted Marches, poured a vial of black water over the map of Eldrimar. Villages hissed and withered beneath the stain, their names dissolving. His goblin generals cheered, but he ignored them, staring instead toward the distant white tower where the last wizard lived. 'Let him send his heroes,' Thornax rumbled. 'I have buried every sword they might carry, and I have taught the mountains to whisper my name.'

General Aurelio Bask seized the radio station at dawn, and by noon the president's portraits were burning in the plaza. He addressed the nation in a crisp white uniform, promising order, bread, and peace. By evening, the lists were ready: teachers, journalists, anyone who had ever laughed at him. He reviewed each name with careful pleasure, as a gardener plans which weeds to pull. 'A country,' he told his aide, 'is simply a house that needs a firm landlord.'

Queen Maelisande of the Frostmere never trusted a gift she had not poisoned herself. At the harvest feast she lifted her goblet, toasting the visiting duke, and watched him drink from the cup she had chosen for him. Her smile did not waver as his fingers began to numb. 'Your lands were always too fertile for a man so foolish,' she whispered, leaning close, while the musicians played on and the court pretended not to see.

Viktor Hollis ran the city's casinos, its police chiefs, and half its newspapers, yet he still checked the locks on his own door each night. Tonight a rival's nephew sat bound in his cellar, unaware he was merely bait. Hollis lit a cigar and waited for the phone to ring. When the rival begged, Hollis would name his price: the docks, the unions, and a public apology. Patience, he thought, was the cruelest weapon he owned.

Atop the crimson citadel, the sorcerer-king Ahzrael stroked the skull-headed scepter and studied the rebels' camp through a pool of blood. He had let their scouts live, let them find the secret pass, let them believe in victory. Now a thousand hidden wraiths waited in the canyon walls. 'Hope is a fine trap,' he told his silent court. 'Feed it generously, and the fools will march into my jaws singing.'

Warlord Dromak Sulle collected the tongues of every messenger who brought bad news, keeping them in jars along his tent's rim. When the scout arrived, pale and shaking, to report the river fortress had held, Sulle only chuckled and offered him wine. The scout drank gratefully. Then Sulle ordered the fortress's children brought before the walls at sunrise, so their parents could watch what stubbornness cost. 'Now,' he said softly, 'let us negotiate.'

Silas Wrenfield arrived in Dunmoor with a trunk of painted bottles and a smile like fresh butter. By dusk he had convinced the miller that his tonic could turn lead into silver, if only the miller would first lend him ten silver coins as "seed." The miller handed them over gladly. By morning, Wrenfield's lodging was empty, the trunk was full of river stones, and the coins were halfway to the coast.

Under the hawthorn, the little man in the green waistcoat offered Briony a bargain. "One year of your laughter for a purse that never empties," he said, grinning with too many teeth. She agreed. The purse was heavy and bright. Only later did she notice that every coin inside was a dry leaf, and that she could not remember how to laugh at all.

Marguerite Dulac shuffled the deck with lazy fingers while the riverboat swayed. She let the planter win twice, sighing as though wounded, then proposed higher stakes. Her left sleeve held the ace of spades, and her smile held nothing. When the final hand was dealt, the planter lost his watch, his ring and his deed to the cotton fields, and Marguerite thanked him sweetly for the lesson.

Tobias Quill sold the village of Harrowgate a bridge it already owned. He wore an official sash, carried a roll of forged blueprints, and spoke gravely of "municipal transfer fees." The elders paid him in installments, each time grateful for his patience. When the real surveyor finally arrived, Quill was gone, leaving behind only a polite thank-you note and a sash stitched from curtain fabric.

The kitsune took the shape of a widow weeping beside the road. When the young merchant Haruto offered his cloak and his company, she thanked him with trembling hands and led him to her "home," a glittering hall of lanterns. He feasted until dawn. Then he woke in a cold bamboo thicket, his cart emptied, his purse stuffed with moss, and distant laughter drifting through the trees.

In the back room of the Gilded Anchor, Dex Calloway rolled the loaded dice once, softly, so they sang the right number. The sailors cheered their own luck. Dex bought them rum, called them brothers, and let them lose just slowly enough to stay hopeful. By midnight their wages were stacked beside his elbow, and he was already planning which port would be fooled next.

Lady Ophelia Vance claimed to be the lost cousin of a duke. She learned his nicknames from gossiping servants, wept convincingly over a miniature portrait she had bought at market, and accepted the household's jewels "for safekeeping" during her supposed illness. When the real cousin's letter arrived, Ophelia had already vanished through the garden gate, humming, with the emeralds sewn into her hem.

The goblin merchant Grizzlewick swore his lantern held a captured star. For three gold pieces, travelers could peer through its tiny shutter and see a glimmer. Nobody noticed the glowworm trapped inside, or the second lantern he swapped in whenever someone demanded to buy it outright. He cackled quietly at his stall, counting coins while the "star" crawled in circles.

Jasper Moon worked the crowded Lisbon train station with a cheerful stumble and a dropped wallet. As a stranger returned it, Jasper insisted on a reward, then on friendship, then on a small loan until his bank opened. Meanwhile his partner's quick hands lightened the stranger's coat. By the time the whistle blew, both thieves had melted into the crowd, laughing behind their scarves.

Old Mother Pell told the villagers she could speak to the dead, and the dead, conveniently, wanted gifts. Candles, silver spoons, a fat goose each winter. She studied funerals for private details, then whispered them in a trembling voice across the séance table. Widows wept and paid. Only the blacksmith's daughter noticed that the ghost never knew anything Pell hadn't already overheard.

Marcus Veyland smiled across the boardroom table as the auditors filed out. The ledgers they had examined were spotless, because he had spent three weeks rewriting them. Now, alone, he slid a folder toward the young accountant who had noticed the discrepancies. "Your mother's care home," he said softly, "is one of our subsidiaries. Funny how fragile contracts can be." The accountant's hands trembled. Veyland poured himself coffee, savoring the silence that meant another problem had quietly become his property.

Delphine Orsay never raised her voice. She simply mailed the senator a single photograph: him, a hotel lobby, a woman who was not his wife. No demand came with it, only a date. For nine days she watched his public statements soften, his votes drift toward her client's pipeline. On the tenth day she sent a second photograph. "Patience is cheaper than ink," she murmured, stirring her tea in a Lisbon café, already composing the next envelope.

Night shift at the Harlow Dam was quiet, which suited Tobias Kerr perfectly. He crouched beside the control cabinet, swapping a sensor board for one he had altered himself. By dawn, the readings would lie, showing calm water while pressure built. His employer, a rival energy firm, would buy the ruined utility for pennies. Kerr tightened the last screw, wiped his fingerprints with a cloth, and strolled past the sleepy guard, whistling a lullaby he hadn't thought of in years.

Ingrid Solberg owned the only copy of the merger files, and she wanted everyone to know it. She called the CEO from a rooftop in Oslo, wind snapping at her coat. "Double my severance, or your shareholders read about the offshore accounts over breakfast." He pleaded; she let him. Then she hung up, checked the second phone in her pocket, and smiled. The real buyer was already bidding higher, and neither man suspected she was playing both.

Everyone at Brightwell Pharmaceuticals thought Dr. Anselm Roake was grieving the failed trial. In truth, he had buried the liver-toxicity data himself. Now he sat in the lab late, shredding pages and feeding emails into a program that would erase their timestamps. When junior researcher Pia knocked, he greeted her warmly, offered tea, and quietly slipped her badge number into a forged report. Someone had to take the fall, he reasoned, and she was conveniently new.

The ferry terminal in Piraeus smelled of diesel and salt. Costas Drakos watched the cargo containers roll past, one marked with a false customs seal he had paid dearly for. Inside: counterfeit heart valves, millions of euros' worth. If hospitals buckled and patients died, that was simply the cost of business. When the inspector approached, Drakos slipped an envelope into her clipboard without breaking his pleasant smile. "Enjoy the sunshine," he said, and walked on.

Vera Lindqvist had been the firm's most trusted security consultant for eleven years, which was exactly why nobody checked her work. She installed the new firewall herself, leaving a hidden door only she could open. Tonight, while the board celebrated a record quarter downstairs, she sat in her car streaming their private files onto a server in Tallinn. By Monday, a competitor would know every bid. She closed her laptop, humming softly, and drove home.

Judge Harlan Pryce's chambers were full of leather and lies. When the prosecutor delivered the file on the shipping magnate, Pryce already knew the verdict he'd been paid to give. He leafed through the evidence slowly, as if considering it. Later, in the parking garage, a man in a gray coat handed him a gym bag. Pryce weighed it in one hand, nodded, and said, "Justice, like wine, benefits from the right vintage."

Nadia Rourke rigged the stadium's lighting grid herself, three nights before the championship. A single signal from her phone would plunge sixty thousand fans into darkness while her accomplices emptied the vault beneath the concession floor. She sat in section 114, eating popcorn and watching the families arrive, children waving banners. Guilt never visited. She checked her watch, counted the minutes to halftime, and let her thumb hover over the glowing screen.

Elliot Brandt had perfected the art of the friendly threat. At the charity gala, he drew the museum director aside, champagne in hand. "Lovely collection. Shame about that provenance on the Vermeer. I'd hate for reporters to learn it was looted." The director paled. Brandt clinked glasses with him, laughing as if they'd shared a joke. "I'll call Tuesday. We'll discuss a donation. A generous one." Then he vanished into the crowd, untouchable.

Old Maragolda lived in a gingerbread cottage at the edge of the Thornwood, and she smiled sweetly at every lost child who knocked. Behind her smile, she counted pots. She fed them honey cakes until their cheeks grew round, whispering to her black cat that the fattest would make the finest stew. Each night she bolted the door and stirred her cauldron, humming a lullaby that smelled faintly of smoke. When the little boy Pell asked why the cellar was full of tiny shoes, she only laughed, and her laugh sounded like dry twigs snapping.

The wolf Ysgrin did not hunt the shepherds' flock by force. He wore a stolen fleece and bleated softly at the pasture gate, and the lambs, trusting, trotted to meet him. Each dusk he chose one, promising a secret meadow of clover beyond the ridge. None returned. The old ram grew suspicious when he noticed the wolf's shadow, long-snouted and thin, stretching wrong across the grass. But Ysgrin only grinned beneath the wool, licking his teeth, and murmured that the ram looked tender enough to be the next to come along.

Grand Vizier Qasimar bowed lower than anyone in the sultan's court, and that was how he hid his dagger-sharp ambition. Each morning he poured the ruler tea and poisoned his mind with whispers: the general plotted treason, the treasurer skimmed gold, the young prince coveted the throne. None of it was true. By winter, the palace was a nest of suspicion, and Qasimar alone seemed loyal. He counted the keys on his belt, one for every door he would soon open, and waited for the sultan's trust to curdle into total, helpless dependence.

In the drowned city of Veshmere, the sea-witch Oru traded in voices. She floated beneath the harbor lanterns and offered fishermen's daughters whatever they longed for: a husband, a ship, a crown of pearls. The price sounded small, only a song. But Oru hid each stolen voice inside a shell on her coral shelf, and at night she listened to them all sing together, a pale chorus of regret. When a girl came begging for her voice back, Oru tilted her head, smiled with needle teeth, and said the contract had no clause for mercy.

The goblin king Brindlethorn loved riddles because he never played them fairly. Travelers crossing his bridge were offered freedom if they answered three questions, but he changed the answers whenever they spoke correctly. A tinker once said 'river,' and Brindlethorn cackled, declaring it was clearly 'rain.' Piles of boots, hats, and bewildered bones lay beneath the bridge. When a clever girl arrived, he rubbed his knobby hands, eager for sport, never guessing she had already noticed the way his left eye twitched whenever he was about to lie.

Sir Aldrewick rode into the village of Hollin with a golden smile and a sealed letter claiming the king had appointed him tax-warden. The villagers, being honest folk, emptied their coffers and fed his horse oats. He never mentioned that the king had died a month earlier, nor that the letter was forged by his own trembling hand. Each night he counted coins by candlelight, practicing a sorrowful speech for the day soldiers came. If anyone grew suspicious, he planned simply to point at the nearest neighbor and shout, 'Thief!'

Beneath the frozen lake lived the Hollow Queen, who borrowed faces. She would rise through cracks in the ice and wear the shape of a lost mother or a drowned sister, calling softly to skaters at twilight. Those who stepped closer felt the ice sigh and open. Her pale hands never hurried. She had learned that grief makes people stupid, and that longing was better bait than any worm. One winter, a boy recognized the voice of his dead father, and the Queen, borrowing the dear familiar smile, held out her arms.

Rikkit the fox boasted that no hen could outwit him, and for once the boast was true. He arrived at the farm dressed as a traveling doctor, carrying a bag of colored bottles. 'Your rooster is ill,' he announced gravely, and prescribed that the henhouse door be left open all night for fresh air. While the farmer nodded, Rikkit winked at his tail, already imagining feathers. By midnight the coop stood open, the moon was bright, and the fox, still in spectacles, crept through the dark with a very large sack.

The sorcerer Dathmoor collected shadows in glass jars, and the village of Lun had begun to notice. People woke feeling thin, cold, and strangely forgetful, their silhouettes fading from walls at noon. Dathmoor sat in his tower, tapping each jar and savoring the whispers of stolen courage, stolen laughter. He had sworn to give everything back after one grand spell, but he lied as easily as he breathed. Now he reached for the jar labeled 'the miller's daughter,' whose shadow was bravest, and which he meant to wear like a cloak.

Every spring the bog-hag Mother Gristle invited travelers to dinner by lighting false lanterns across the marsh. Wanderers followed the friendly glow, stumbling deeper into mud, until her long arms rose to drag them under. She kept their boots as trophies and polished their buttons until they shone. When the tin peddler Orsolo spotted the lights, he smelled rot beneath the sweetness and grew wary. Mother Gristle, watching from the reeds, only blew on the lanterns harder, sighing a lonesome tune that promised warm bread and a bed for the weary.
